title: Ad Nationes Libri Duo
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa002.opp-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Denique Socrates ex ea parte damnatus est, qua propius temptaverat veritatem, deos vestros destruendo. Quamquam nondum tunc in terris nomen Christianum, tamen veritas semper damnabatur. Itaque et sapientem non negabitis cui etiam Pythius vester testimonium dixerat. Virorum, inquit, omnium Socrates sapientissimus. Vicit Apollinem veritas, ut ipse adversus se pronuntiaret; confessus est enim se deum non esse, sed eum quoque sapientissimum affirmans qui deos abnuebat. Porro apud vos eo minus sapiens, quia deos abnuens, cum ideo sapiens, quia deos ab(??)ens.
passages.english: In fact Socrates was condemned on that very count by which he had come nearer to the truth, by destroying your gods. Although the Christian name was not yet on earth at that time, still the truth was always being condemned. And so you will not deny that he was wise, to whom even your Pythian [god] had borne witness: "Of all men," he said, "Socrates is the wisest." Truth overcame Apollo, so that he pronounced against himself; for he confessed that he was not a god, by affirming that the man who rejected the gods was also the wisest. Yet among you he is the less wise because he rejected the gods, when [in fact] he was wise precisely because he rejected the gods.
passages.notes: The last word is damaged in the text ("ab(??)ens"); read as "abnuens" (rejecting), repeating the earlier participle.

passages.original: Ubi tunc Christiani, cum res Romana tot historias laborum suorum subministravit? Ubi tunc Christiani, cum Hiera, Anaphe et Delos et Rhodos et Cea insulae multis cum milibus hominum pessum ierunt, vel quam Plato memorat maiorem Asia aut Africa in Atlantico mari mersam? cum Vulsinios de caelo, Pompeios de suo monte perfudit ignis? cum terrae motu mare Corinthium ereptum est? cum totum orbem cataclysmus abolevit? Ubi tunc, non dicam contemptores deorum Christiani, sed ipsi dei vestri, quos clade illa posteriores loca, oppida approbant in quibus nati, morati, sepulti sunt, etiam quae condiderunt?
passages.english: Where were the Christians then, when the Roman state supplied so many histories of its troubles? Where were the Christians then, when the islands Hiera, Anaphe, Delos, Rhodes and Cea went to destruction with many thousands of people, or the one which Plato records, larger than Asia or Africa, sunk in the Atlantic sea? When fire from heaven drenched Volsinii, and fire from its own mountain Pompeii? When the Corinthian sea was snatched away by an earthquake? When the deluge wiped out the whole world? Where then were, I will not say the Christians, despisers of the gods, but your gods themselves, whom places and towns later than that disaster vouch for, [towns] in which they were born, lived and were buried, and even those which they founded?
passages.notes: "mare Corinthium ereptum est" is obscure; it may refer to the sea being withdrawn or to land breaking through at the Isthmus. "Quos clade illa posteriores loca... approbant" is compressed. The sense seems to be that the gods' own birthplaces and tombs postdate the flood, so the gods are later than it.

passages.original: Certe Liberum Patrem cum sacris suis consules senatus auctoritate non urbe solummodo, verum tota Italia eliminaverunt. Ceterum Serapem et Isidem et Arpocraten et Anubem prohibitos Capitolio Varro commemorat, eorumque aras a senatu deiectas nonnisi per vim popularium restructas. Sed tamen et Gabinius consul Kalendis Ianuariis, cum vix hostias probaret prae popularium coetu, quia nihil de Serape et Iside constituisset, potiorem habuit senatus censuram quam impetum vulgi, et aras institui prohibuit.
passages.english: Certainly the consuls, on the authority of the senate, banished Father Liber together with his rites not only from the city but from all Italy. Moreover Varro records that Serapis and Isis and Harpocrates and Anubis were forbidden the Capitol, and that their altars, thrown down by the senate, were rebuilt only through the violence of the populace. But even so the consul Gabinius, on the Kalends of January, when he could scarcely approve the sacrificial victims because of the crowd of the populace, since he had made no decision about Serapis and Isis, held the senate's judgement weightier than the onslaught of the mob, and forbade the altars to be set up.

passages.original: Xenocrates Academicus bifariam facit, Olympios et Titanios, qui de Caelo et Terra. Aegyptiorum plerique quattuor deos credunt, Solem et Lunam, Caelum ac Terram. Cum reliquo igni superno deos ortos Democritus suspicatur, cuius instar vult esse naturam Zenon. Unde et Varro ignem mundi animum facit, ut perinde in mundo ignis omnia gubernet sicut animus in nobis. Atqui vanissime. Nam cum est, inquit, in nobis, ipsi sumus; cum exivit, emorimur.
passages.english: Xenocrates the Academic makes [them] twofold, Olympians and Titans, who [are sprung] from Heaven and Earth. Most of the Egyptians believe in four gods: Sun and Moon, Heaven and Earth. Democritus conjectures that the gods arose together with the rest of the fire above, and Zeno wants nature to be like this [fire]. Hence Varro too makes fire the soul of the world, so that fire governs all things in the world just as the soul does in us. But this is most foolish. For when it is in us, he says, we ourselves exist; when it has gone out, we die.
passages.notes: "inquit" ("he says") may refer to Varro, or it may be Tertullian's imagined objector. The argument is a reductio: if fire is the world's soul, then fire leaving the world through lightning would mean the world dies.

passages.original: Itaque quod mundi erit, hoc elementis adscribetur, caelo dico et terrae et sideribus et igni, quae deos et deorum parentes adversus negatam generationem dei et nativitatem frustra vobis credi proposuit Varro, ut qui Varro indicaverat animalia esse caelum et astra. Quod si ita est, etiam mortalia sint necesse est, secundum animalis formam; nam etsi immortalem constat animam, ipsi hoc soli licebit, non etiam illi cui adnectatur, id est corpori.
passages.english: So whatever belongs to the world will be ascribed to the elements—I mean the sky and the earth and the stars and fire—which Varro proposed, in vain, that you should believe to be gods and parents of gods, against the denial of generation and birth to a god; for Varro had declared that the sky and the stars are living beings. But if that is so, they must also be mortal, in accordance with the form of a living being; for even if the soul is agreed to be immortal, this will be allowed to it alone, not also to that to which it is joined, that is, the body.

passages.original: Quin ergo ad humaniorem aliquanto convertimur opinionem, quae de communi omnium sensu et simplici coniectura deducta videatur? Nam et Varro meminit eius, creditam praeterea dicens elementorum divinitatem, quod nihil omnino sine suffragio illorum gigni, ali, provehi possit ad vitae humanae et terrae sationem, quando ne ipsa quidem corpora aut animas sufficere licuisset sine elementorum temperamento, quo habitatio ista mundi circulorum condicionibus foederata praestatur, nisi quod hominum incolatui denegavit enormitas frigoris aut caloris, proptereaque deos credi solem, qui diei de suo cumulet, fruges caloribus maturet, annum stationibus servet: lunam, solatium noctium, patrocinium mensum gubernaculis: item sidera, signacula quaedam temporum ad rurationem notandorum: ipsum denique caelum, sub quo omnia, terram, super quam omnia, et quicquid illorum inter se ad commoda humana conspirat.
passages.english: Why then do we not turn to a somewhat more human opinion, one which seems to be drawn from the common sense of all and from simple conjecture? For Varro too mentions it, saying that the divinity of the elements was believed besides because nothing at all could be begotten, nourished, or brought forward for the sowing of human life and of the earth without their support, since not even bodies themselves or souls could have been sustained without the tempering of the elements, by which this dwelling of the world, bound by the conditions of its zones, is provided—except where the excess of cold or heat has denied it to human habitation; and that for this reason the sun was believed a god, because it fills up the day from its own [light], ripens the crops with its heat, and keeps the year by its stations; the moon, the comfort of the nights, the patron of the months by its governance; likewise the stars, certain signs of the seasons to be marked for tilling the fields; and finally the sky itself, under which all things are, the earth, upon which all things are, and whatever among them works together for human benefit.

passages.original: Nam quae idonea auctoritas praecucurrit eiusmodi theologiae quam etiam fama destituit? Quanti sunt qui norint visu vel auditu Atargatim Syrorum, Caelestem Afrorum, Varsutinam Maurorum, Obodan et Dusarem Arabum, Belenum Noricum, vel quos Varro ponit: Casiniensium Deluentinum, Nar- niensium Visidianum, Atinensium Numiternum, Asculanorum Anchariam, et quam perceperint Vulsiniensium Nortiam, quorum ne nominum quidem dignitas humanis cognominibus distat?
passages.english: For what adequate authority has gone before a theology of this kind, which even report has abandoned? How many are there who know by sight or hearing Atargatis of the Syrians, Caelestis of the Africans, Varsutina of the Moors, Obodas and Dusares of the Arabs, Belenus of Noricum, or those whom Varro lists: Deluentinus of the people of Casinum, Visidianus of the people of Narnia, Numiternus of the people of Atina, Ancharia of the people of Asculum, and Nortia of the people of Volsinii, whom they have come to know—gods whose names are not even superior in dignity to human surnames?
passages.notes: "et quam perceperint" is awkward; rendered loosely.

passages.original: Sed enim manifestis vis sua adsistit. Quos a primordio possunt non asserere nisi homines fuisse, recipiunt in divinitatem, affirmando illos post mortem deos factos, ut Varro, et qui cum eo somniaverunt. Hic igitur consisto: si sunt allecti dei vestri in hoc nomen et numen, ut in ordinem senatorium, sapientia vestra esse concedatis iam necesse est aliquem summum dominatorem habentem allegandi potestatem et quasi Caesarem;
passages.english: But indeed what is evident has its own force. Those whom from the beginning they cannot claim to have been anything but men, they receive into divinity, by asserting that they were made gods after death, as Varro does, and those who dreamed along with him. Here, then, I take my stand: if your gods were co-opted into this name and godhead, as into the senatorial order, you must now in your wisdom concede that there is some supreme ruler who has the power of co-opting, a kind of Caesar;

passages.original: Qui tunc dignius rogo sese inrogasset prae dolore parricidiorum, qui uxoris ob lasciviam venenis circumventus magis meruit ut inho- nesta morte moreretur, hunc vos de pyra in caelum sublevdstis, illa facilitate qua et alium ignis ex divini vi confectum, qui pauca experientiae ingenia commentus dicebatur mortuos ad vitam recurasse. Is Apollinis filius, tam homo quam Iovis nepos, Saturni pronepos (vel potius spurius ut incerto patre, ut Argivus Socrates detulit, quippe expositum repertum, turpius Iove educatum, canino scilicet ubere), merito, id quod nemo negare potest, fulmine haustus est. Malus Iuppiter Optimus hic rursus est, impius in nepotem, invidus in artificem.
passages.english: He who at that time would more fittingly have cast himself onto the pyre out of grief for his murders of kin, who, caught by poison through his wife's wantonness, rather deserved to die a dishonourable death—him you raised from the pyre to heaven, with the same ease with which [you raised] another, destroyed by fire through divine force, who was said, having devised a few clever methods from experience, to have restored the dead to life. He was the son of Apollo, as much a man as [he was] grandson of Jupiter and great-grandson of Saturn (or rather a bastard, as being of uncertain father, as Socrates of Argos reported, since he was found exposed, and more shamefully reared than Jupiter, namely at a dog's teat); deservedly, as no one can deny, he was swallowed up by the thunderbolt. Here again Jupiter the Best is bad: impious toward his grandson, envious toward the craftsman.
passages.notes: First sentence refers to Hercules; the second figure is Aesculapius. "ex divini vi" read as "ex divina vi"; "sublevdstis" as "sublevastis". The phrase "pauca experientiae ingenia commentus" is obscure.
